# Design decisions

## Phase 1 — Backend scaffold, models, migrations, FTS5

**Python 3.12 via uv.** The machine's system Python is 3.9; the plan asks for 3.11+. `uv venv --python 3.12` gives an isolated interpreter without touching the system.

**Migrations are the only way the schema is created.** `0001` is autogenerated from the models and reviewed; `0002` is hand-written SQL for the FTS5 table and triggers, since Alembic cannot model virtual tables. The app runs `alembic upgrade head` on startup (so a fresh Railway volume self-initializes) and the tests build their DB the same way, so triggers are covered by tests rather than assumed. `alembic check` reports no drift between models and migrations.

**Foreign keys are enforced per-connection.** SQLite ignores FKs (and therefore `ON DELETE CASCADE`) unless `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` is set on every connection. `make_engine` does this in a connect listener; both the app and Alembic use it. WAL mode is also enabled for concurrent reads during writes.

**FTS5 is external-content, keyed by segment id.** The index stores no second copy of the text; it reads it back from `transcript_segments` (`content_rowid='id'`). The plan listed a `segment_id UNINDEXED` column, but with external content the FTS rowid *is* the segment id, so a separate column would be redundant and would have to exist on the base table. `meeting_id` is kept `UNINDEXED` so hits can be grouped by meeting without tokenizing it.
- Tokenizer is `porter unicode61`, so "deploying" matches "deploy".
- Three triggers (insert / delete / update-of-text) keep the index in sync. External-content tables require replaying the *old* values through the special `'delete'` command on removal, otherwise the index silently drifts.
- A test confirms these triggers also fire when segments disappear via `ON DELETE CASCADE` from a meeting delete — this is the case most likely to leave ghost search hits.

**Enums are VARCHAR + CHECK.** SQLite has no enum type; `native_enum=False, create_constraint=True` stores the string value and rejects invalid ones at the DB level (tested).

**Naming convention on constraints.** Deterministic names let Alembic batch mode alter SQLite tables later (SQLite can't `ALTER` constraints in place).

**Choices where the plan was silent:**
- `transcript_segments.participant_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL` and nullable, so a transcript survives if a participant is removed.
- `meeting_participants.person_id` has no cascade: deleting a meeting must never delete a `people` row (tested).
- `people.email` uses a plain `UNIQUE`: SQLite treats NULLs as distinct, which is exactly "unique where not null".
- `meetings(owner_id, started_at)` is a plain index rather than `started_at DESC`; SQLite scans a b-tree backward at no cost.
- Summary `keywords` is a JSON column (SQLite JSON1), not a join table, since it is always read and written as a whole.

## Phase 2 — Seed data

**Seed content is authored as JSON; timestamps are computed.** Each file in `backend/app/seed/data/` holds speaker/text pairs, not hand-typed millisecond values. `services/timing.py` lays segments out at 150 words/min (400 ms/word) with a 600 ms pause between turns and a 1.5 s minimum. This keeps the data readable and diffable, and guarantees ordered, non-overlapping integer-ms timings. The same function will be reused for plain `.txt` uploads in Phase 3, which the plan also specifies at ~150 wpm, so there is one definition of "synthesized timing".

**Chapters, action items and soundbites point at segment indices (`at`), not times.** The seeder resolves them to `start_ms` and real `transcript_segments.id`s. That means `action_items.source_segment_id` (click-to-jump) is populated for every seeded item, and the references can't drift from the transcript. A pydantic validator in `seed/loader.py` rejects unknown speakers, out-of-range indices and out-of-order chapters, so a typo fails at load time with the file name instead of seeding a broken meeting. Several indices were wrong on my first pass; auditing each against the segment text caught them, and the validator now guards range errors.

**Seven meetings, one recurring cast.** Standup (4 speakers, 21 turns), sales discovery call (4, 44), engineering interview (3, 44), product review (5, 51), 1:1 (2, 31), incident postmortem (4, 39), campaign planning (5, 37). Twelve people appear across 27 participations, e.g. the default user Alex Morgan is in five meetings. This is deliberate: it makes the `people` table, "filter by participant", and the same-person-across-meetings design point demonstrable instead of theoretical. Meeting content cross-references itself (the postmortem mentions Northwind from the sales call; the 1:1 follows from the postmortem's on-call load) so the library reads like one team's real week.

**Idempotency rule: seed only when there are zero users.** Counting meetings would re-seed if someone deleted every meeting; counting users means demo data returns only on a genuinely fresh database (e.g. a new Railway volume). `python -m app.seed.seed --reset` wipes and reseeds explicitly. Reset deletes users first (cascading to meetings and participants), then people and tags, because `meeting_participants.person_id` deliberately has no cascade.

**Seeding runs on startup** (`SEED_ON_STARTUP`, default on) after migrations, per the deployment note that the demo must never show a blank app. Tests point `DB_PATH` at a temp directory before any app import so they never touch the dev database.

**Deviations from the plan:**
- Seeded meetings have `media_url = NULL`, so the Phase 6 player will use the simulated-clock fallback. The plan called for one shared royalty-free audio file, but I can't responsibly pick and download audio without you choosing the source, and a real recording wouldn't match 3–7 minute synthesized timings anyway. A single file can be dropped in later by setting `media_url`.
- Lengths run 2.8 to 7.1 minutes rather than "realistic" 30-minute meetings. Writing transcripts that long by hand is low value; the 2.5x spread in length still exercises list sorting, duration display and scrolling.
- The 1:1 has 2 speakers (plan said 3–5); a three-person 1:1 isn't a 1:1.

## Phase 3 — API, services, parser, tests

**Layering is enforced by file, not by convention.** Routers (`app/routers/`) only bind HTTP to a service call and a response schema. All logic lives in `app/services/`; the only raw SQL is the FTS5 queries in `search_service.py` (FTS5 `MATCH`, `snippet()`, `highlight()` and `bm25()` have no ORM equivalent). Services take the owning `User` explicitly, so every query is scoped by `owner_id` even though there is only one user today.

**One error shape.** `{"detail", "code"}` for everything: app errors (`AppError`), unknown routes/405s, request validation, and Pydantic errors raised inside handlers. `code` is machine-readable (`not_found`, `validation_error`, `invalid_transcript`, `participant_conflict`, `llm_not_configured`, ...) so the frontend can branch on it and toast `detail`. Routes declare `ErrorOut` in OpenAPI.

**Datetimes are timezone-aware end to end (`UTCDateTime`).** SQLite has no time zones and SQLAlchemy returns naive values, which would serialize as `2026-10-06T09:30:00` — browsers read that as *local* time, shifting every meeting by the viewer's offset. A `TypeDecorator` attaches UTC on read and normalizes on write. It changes no DDL (`alembic check` is clean), and a test asserts every timestamp ends in `Z`.

**Transcript parser (`services/transcript_parser/`)** is one small module per format feeding a shared `finalize()` that resolves all timings to integer ms.
- *txt*: `[hh:mm:ss] Speaker: text`, `Speaker (hh:mm:ss): text`, `hh:mm:ss Speaker: text`, bare `Speaker: text`, wrapped continuation lines, and a lone `[timestamp]` line stamping the next line. A `Label:` only starts a new speaker turn if it looks like a name (1-4 capitalised words, or an already-seen speaker, not `Note:`/`Agenda:`), so "Here's the plan: ..." inside a paragraph is not mistaken for a speaker.
- *vtt/srt*: one cue parser (comma vs dot milliseconds, optional hours, `<v Name>` voice tags, `Name:` prefixes, HTML entities/tags stripped, speakers inherited from the previous cue, NOTE/STYLE/REGION skipped).
- *json*: accepts a list or `{segments|transcript|utterances|...: [...]}`, several key spellings, numeric speaker ids, `"00:01:05"` strings. **Seconds vs milliseconds** is detected: `*_ms` keys are always ms; any fractional value means seconds; otherwise a median utterance length under 100 units means seconds (100 ms is not a plausible utterance). This heuristic can be wrong for odd data, so explicit `start_ms`/`end_ms` keys are the escape hatch.
- Missing timestamps are interpolated; missing ends become `start + estimated speaking time`, clamped to the next start. With no timestamps at all, `services/timing.py` synthesizes ~150 wpm (shared with the seed).
- Control characters are stripped from text because the search layer uses `\x02`/`\x03` as highlight sentinels; this keeps splitting unambiguous.
- Limits: 5 MB, 20,000 segments, UTF-8 only, extensions `.txt .vtt .srt .json .md`. Every failure is a `TranscriptParseError` with a message meant to be shown to the user.

**Creating a meeting is synchronous.** Parse -> people -> participants -> segments -> summary -> `ready` in one request. There is no background queue because the heuristic summary takes milliseconds and the plan has no real speech-to-text; a job queue would be complexity with no benefit. If summary generation raises, the transcript is kept, status becomes `failed`, and `POST .../summary/regenerate` repairs it (tested). Bad input fails *before* anything is written (tested: nothing half-created).

**`POST /api/meetings` takes JSON or multipart** by inspecting `Content-Type`, because FastAPI cannot route two bodies to one path declaratively. OpenAPI documents both via `openapi_extra`. One gotcha worth remembering: `request.form()` yields Starlette's `UploadFile`, not FastAPI's subclass, so `isinstance` must use the Starlette class. The unused `source='form'` enum value is reserved; paste -> `paste`, file -> `upload`.

**People resolution.** A speaker label reuses an existing person by email, else by case-insensitive name. Generic labels (`Speaker 2`, `Guest`, `Unknown`) never merge — merging every "Speaker 1" across meetings would corrupt the people list and the participant filter. `PATCH` lets the user re-point a speaker at an existing person or a new name (the original `speaker_label` is kept, since it records what the source transcript said); pointing two speakers at one person is a 409.

**Search.** User text is never passed to FTS5 raw: words are individually quoted (so `AND`, `NEAR(`, `-`, `*`, stray quotes cannot raise syntax errors — tested with hostile input), `"quoted phrases"` stay phrases, and the last bare word is a prefix match for type-ahead. Results are ranked by `bm25`. Snippets and in-meeting match offsets come from SQLite's own `snippet()`/`highlight()`, so highlighting is stem-aware ("deploy" highlights "deploying"), which a client-side regex could not do. The API returns structured `[{text, match}]` parts rather than HTML, so the frontend never needs `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` on user-controlled transcript text. Offsets are Python code-point indices; they differ from JS UTF-16 indices only for characters outside the BMP (emoji), a known edge.

**Action items and regenerate.** PATCH uses `model_fields_set`, so omitted fields are untouched while an explicit `null` clears assignee/due date. `completed_at` is set on the false->true transition only. An assignee or source segment from another meeting is rejected (422). Regenerating the summary replaces overview, keywords and outline, but never deletes or edits action items (they are user data); it only appends suggestions whose normalized text isn't already present, so regenerate is idempotent.

**Heuristic summarizer.** Chapters are fixed time windows (window = duration/6 clamped to 1-10 min, sparse windows merged), titled by their top TF-IDF terms; keywords are TF-IDF over those windows with speaker names excluded; the overview is the first substantive sentence of each chapter; action items come from regexes (`I'll`, `we need to`, `can you`, `by Friday`, `action item`, `make sure`, `follow up`), with the speaker as assignee for first-person commitments, the *next* speaker for "can you ...?", deadlines resolved relative to the meeting date, and questions/pleasantries filtered out. Honest limitation: chapter titles are keyword lists ("Staging, Million, Scans"), not prose — that is what the LLM path is for.

**LLM is pluggable and never required.** `LLM_API_KEY` unset -> `get_llm_client()` returns `None` and everything uses the heuristic. When set, the official `anthropic` SDK is used (default model `claude-opus-5-5`, overridable with `LLM_MODEL`). Any LLM failure (rate limit, auth, refusal, truncation, malformed JSON, out-of-range indices) raises `LLMError` and summaries silently fall back to the heuristic; `/ask` instead returns 502 with the reason. Transcripts over 400k characters are not truncated; they fall back/422. **Not exercised against the real API** (no key here): the wrapper is tested with a fake SDK object and the real SDK's exception classes, and the prompt/JSON contract is tested with a fake client.

**Export** is Markdown or plain text built from the same loaders as the detail page, served with `Content-Disposition` and a slugified filename.

**Testing approach.** 186 tests. Fixtures build each test's database with the real Alembic migrations (so FTS triggers are live), override `get_db` and the LLM dependency, and run the real app through `TestClient`. Parser tests are table-driven including malformed input; API tests assert status codes *and* the error body shape, cascade behaviour (including FTS cleanup), filter combinations, pagination without overlap, and that a failed PATCH leaves no partial change.

## Phase 4 — Frontend shell

**Stack as planned: Next.js (App Router, TS), Tailwind v4, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query, sonner, lucide-react.** Versions are current as of the build (Next 16.4, React 19, Tailwind 4). Because Next 16 differs from older releases, I read the bundled docs in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` rather than relying on memory; that caught one real difference (the `error.tsx` prop is `retry`, not `reset`/`unstable_retry`). shadcn's current default is the Base UI flavour, so triggers use a `render` prop instead of Radix's `asChild`. Its `cn` helper comes from the `cn` package published by the shadcn maintainer (verified, not a typosquat).

**Types are generated, not hand-written.** `npm run gen:types` runs `openapi-typescript` against the backend's `/openapi.json` into `lib/api-types.ts`; `lib/types.ts` only gives friendly aliases. The backend schemas are the single source of truth, so a renamed field breaks `tsc` instead of breaking at runtime.

**Theme tokens come from the reference.** Colours were sampled from `docs/reference/` screenshots (page `#131314`, surface `#1e1e1f`, card `#19191a`, border `#292929`, primary `#623ae6`) and exposed as CSS variables mapped into Tailwind (`bg-background`, `bg-surface`, `bg-primary`, ...), so components never hard-code a colour and Phase 8's dark/light switch is a token swap. The `.dark` block is the reference look and the app currently always renders dark; the `:root` light block is provisional and gets finished and verified in Phase 8. Speaker colours (`speaker-0..5`) are defined now for the transcript.

**Shell layout follows the screenshots:** a 232 px sidebar that collapses to a 56 px icon rail (state kept in `localStorage` through `useSyncExternalStore`, so there is no hydration mismatch and storage failures just fall back to expanded), a 52 px top bar with title, a centred search field and a primary action, and the account menu as the sidebar's header (as in the reference). Below the `md` breakpoint the same sidebar is shown in a drawer that closes on navigation. The sidebar lists only pages that exist; Tasks and Analytics link to honest "Soon" placeholders, so there are no dead links.

**Deliberately not copied from the reference:** the plan/usage meter, "Upgrade", notification bell, Capture button, theme and logout rows. This app has one demo user, no billing and no auth, and a control that does nothing is worse than no control. The top-bar primary button is "Upload" (this app's real entry point). The logo is an original mark, not Fireflies' asset.

**Search box** submits to `/search?q=`, mirrors the query back from the URL (keyed so it resets on navigation without an effect), and focuses on Cmd/Ctrl+K.

**Cold-start handling (plan section 9).** `useBackendStatus` polls `/api/health`: after 2.5 s without an answer a banner says the server is waking up; if the request fails it says the API can't be reached and retries every 4 s until it recovers. TanStack Query pauses that polling in a hidden tab, which is the right behaviour. Verified by stopping and restarting the backend.

**`cacheComponents` / `partialPrefetching` are turned off.** `create-next-app` enabled them. With them on, the production build failed on `/meetings/[id]`: anything reading the URL (`usePathname` in the shell) must sit inside `<Suspense>` on dynamic routes. They suit server-fetched pages; this app fetches everything on the client with TanStack Query, so they only add constraints. Worth knowing: `next dev` did not surface this, only `next build` did, so the build is part of the verification.

**API client.** A thin typed `fetch` wrapper: query-string building that skips empty values, `FormData` passthrough so the browser sets the multipart boundary, `204` handling, and every failure surfaces as `ApiError{status, code, message}` using the backend's `{detail, code}` body. Network failures become status 0 / `network_error`, since `fetch` only rejects on those. Unit-tested.

**Verification.** `tsc`, `eslint`, 14 vitest tests (time formatting round-trips, API client behaviours) and a production build all pass. In the browser: root redirect, live user and library count from the API, active-route highlighting, search navigation, the drawer, and the offline banner. Note for future browser testing: with viewport emulation on, the browser tool double-scales clicks that target elements by reference, so they can land on the wrong element; test at the pane's natural size or click by screenshot coordinates.

## Phase 5 — Meetings library

**The URL is the filter state.** `q`, `participant_id`, `tag`, `from`, `to`, `sort`, `page` live in the query string and `lib/library-filters.ts` is the only code that encodes/decodes them (parse is forgiving: malformed values fall back to defaults instead of erroring; encode omits defaults so a clean library has a clean URL; 19 unit tests including round-trips). Refresh, share-a-link and the back button all work; verified by driving the real router (each discrete filter change is a history `push`, typing is a `replace`, so the back button steps through filter changes without a history entry per keystroke).

**Typed text is debounced (300 ms) into the URL, and the box follows the URL back.** Clearing a chip or pressing Back changes `q` from outside, so `LibrarySearch` distinguishes "the URL changed because I wrote it" from "it changed for another reason" and only overwrites the input in the second case. Without that, characters typed during the round trip got overwritten.

**Server-side everything.** Filtering, sorting and pagination all run in the API (`GET /api/meetings`); the client never filters a list in memory. The text filter matches titles and transcript text (FTS5), which the top-bar search deliberately does not duplicate: that one goes to `/search` for ranked, highlighted results across transcripts.

**Layout from the reference.** Left panel is this app's "channels" (All meetings + one row per tag with counts, from `/api/tags`); toolbar = text filter, Filters popover (participant, tag, date range, with a count badge), sort; removable chips show every active filter; meetings are grouped under day headings (Today, Yesterday, "Tue, Oct 6") when the sort is by date and shown flat when sorted by title or duration. Native `<select>`/`<input type=date>` are used inside the popover: accessible, keyboard- and mobile-friendly, and nothing to break.

**Four distinct empty/error states:** library empty (CTA to add a meeting), filters matched nothing (Clear filters), page number past the end (Back to first page), request failed (message from the API + retry). `placeholderData: keepPreviousData` keeps the old list (dimmed) while a new filter loads instead of flashing a skeleton.

**A real bug the browser caught: hydration mismatch.** The library sits in a `<Suspense>` boundary (required by `useSearchParams`), and Suspense boundaries hydrate *after* the rest of the page. By then the account menu had already put the library count in the shared TanStack Query cache, so the library's first client render showed a count the server HTML didn't have. `useHydrated()` makes data-driven page content render its skeleton on the first client render so it always matches the server. Rule for later pages: anything inside a Suspense boundary that reads the query cache is gated on `useHydrated()`.

**Pagination** is 20 per page with Previous/Next and "21–22 of 22"; verified against a temporary 22-meeting library (page 1 = 20, page 2 = 2, Previous returns to page 1, Previous disabled on page 1), then cleaned up.

## Phase 6 — Meeting detail

**One clock drives everything.** `PlayerController` owns a position in milliseconds and is backed either by the real `<audio>/<video>` element or, when a meeting has no media, by a simulated clock. The transcript, chapters and player bar only read that position, so a meeting without a recording behaves the same as one with it. The active transcript line is found with a binary search over segment start times (unit-tested), not a scan per tick.

**Deep links are first-class.** `?t=<ms>` seeks on load; Ask Fred sources and search results link to it, so every citation lands on the moment it came from.

**Optimistic action items.** Ticking an item updates the cache immediately and rolls back with a toast if the request fails (checked by taking the backend away mid-click). Everything else waits for the server.

**Responsive rule.** At `xl` the page is three columns (transcript | notes | Ask Fred); between `lg` and `xl` Ask Fred becomes a button + sheet; below `lg` the three panels are tabs.

## Phase 7 — Create, edit, delete, upload

**Transcript parsing is a package of small parsers** (timed cues for VTT/SRT, plain `Name: text`, JSON) behind one entry point, table-tested including malformed input. A bad file raises a `TranscriptParseError` with a specific message (for example the JSON line of a syntax error) rather than a generic 422.

**People are deduplicated per owner**, preferring a person with an email when names collide, and people left with no meetings are cleaned up so the filter list stays honest.

**Upload shows real progress** (XHR, since `fetch` has no upload progress) and the media endpoint streams with `Range` support so seeking works.

## Phase 8 — Polish

**Light theme is a token swap**, verified on the library and detail pages; the theme is applied by an inline script before first paint so there is no dark flash, and is stored locally and in the account settings.

**Honest placeholders.** Anything that would need infrastructure this app does not have (calendar bots, live assist, teams, MCP, most integrations) is labelled "Coming soon" or "Not part of this version" and is not interactive. A control that does nothing is worse than no control.

## Phase 9 — Search, tasks, analytics

**Search uses the FTS5 index** with `porter unicode61` so "deploying" finds "deploy". Results are segments with highlighted snippets and a deep link; the query is sanitised into a safe FTS expression (user input never reaches `MATCH` raw).

**Tasks and analytics are read-only aggregations** in `insights` services, scoped to the owner. Talk time is computed from segment durations per speaker.

## Phase 10 — Docs and deploy

README (setup, architecture, schema, API, limits) and `docs/DEPLOY.md`. The backend ships as a Dockerfile because SQLite needs a persistent volume (`/data`) and Railway mounts one per service. `APP_ENV=production` refuses to start with the default secret key.

## Accounts, ownership and security (added after Phase 5)

**Built-in auth instead of a vendor.** Email + password with scrypt hashes, short-lived JWTs in an `Authorization` header, optional Google sign-in with a verified ID token, and a seeded demo account. This needs no external signup to run, and swapping in a hosted provider later only touches `deps.current_user`. Trade-off: we own password reset and throttling (in memory, so per instance).

**Reset tokens are bound to the password they replace**: the token carries a fingerprint of the current hash, so using it once (or changing the password another way) invalidates it.

**Ownership is a column, not a convention.** `owner_id` on meetings, people and tags; every service query takes the owner. A request for someone else's meeting returns 404, not 403, so ids are not probeable. Migration `0003` backfills existing rows to the demo user and runs with foreign keys off, because SQLite's batch table rebuild otherwise cascade-deleted child rows (found on the real dev database; `test_migrations.py` pins it).

**API keys** (`ffk_…`) are shown once, stored only as a SHA-256 hash with a short prefix for display, and authenticate exactly like a login token.

**Media links are signed and versioned** (`?sig=&v=`), because `<audio src>` cannot send a bearer header; replacing a file changes `v` so browsers do not serve the old one.

**Webhooks are SSRF-guarded:** HTTPS only, hostnames resolved and rejected if private/loopback/link-local, no redirects, and bodies signed with `X-Signature` (HMAC-SHA256 with a per-integration secret).

## Email

**Transports: SMTP, Resend, or log.** With no credentials the app still renders every email and stores it in `email_log`, shown in the in-app outbox with a sandboxed preview. That makes the feature demonstrable and testable without a mail account, and it is clearly labelled as "not sent" so nobody assumes delivery.

**Sent in a background task** after the response, so a slow mail server never slows an upload. The recap respects settings (to me, to participants, what to include) and carries the compliance notice when configured.

## Settings

**Settings are one JSON document per user, validated server-side** with unknown keys rejected, so a typo in the client fails loudly instead of silently saving nothing. The UI mirrors the reference's grouped left nav; rows for features that do not exist are visibly disabled.

## Ask Fred

**Works without a model.** With no `LLM_API_KEY` the "search" mode answers with the best-matching transcript lines and their timestamps (and says so in the panel). With a key, answers are written by the model from retrieved segments only, and the system prompt tells it to treat transcript and knowledge-base text as data, not instructions. The global panel in the library uses the same component with `meetingId = null`.

## Shell parity with the reference (Home, AskFred, profile panel)

**This reverses an earlier call.** In Phase 4 I left out the plan chip, Upgrade, bell, Capture button and the profile panel's extra rows because they would have been controls that did nothing. You asked for the same look, so they are back, but each one is wired to something real or says plainly that it is not available:

- **Sidebar** now follows the reference: Home, AskFred | Meetings, Tasks, AI Skills | Analytics, Voice Agents | Upgrade, then Try Email Assistant, Integrations, Settings and the dismissible "Create Team" card. Upload and Search left the sidebar (the Capture menu and the top-bar search cover them; the routes still exist).
- **Top bar:** the plan chip shows the real meeting count, Upgrade opens a page that says there are no plans, the bell lists the emails the app actually sent (red dot until opened), and Capture is a split button to the upload and paste flows. "Record a live meeting" is disabled and labelled.
- **Profile panel** is the two-column popover. The plan and storage figures are real (meeting count, minutes from the analytics totals); Theme cycles dark/light/system and saves; the right-hand cards point at API keys, Integrations and the API docs instead of Fireflies' mobile, Chrome and desktop apps, which do not exist here. Playlist is disabled ("Coming soon").
- **Home** is the post-login landing page (`HOME_PATH`): welcome card, Quick Start, Recent / Upcoming / AI Feed tabs (recent meetings, an honest "no calendar" empty state, open action items) and Try More.
- **AskFred** is a full page with a chat list kept in this browser's localStorage. **AI Skills** are one-click prompts that open a new AskFred chat (`/askfred?q=`), so they really work. **Voice Agents** reproduces the layout but every card is labelled "Not available".
- The promo banner says what this build offers rather than advertising a trial that does not exist.

## Second parity pass: Home, meetings, channels, AI Skills, analytics

**Home is the returning-user page.** After the first pass I had copied the new-user welcome screen. Home now follows the real one: greeting, Personal Assistant cards (Daily Brief opens a prefilled AskFred chat, Tasks shows the real open count, Meeting Prep says there is no calendar), Recent / Upcoming / AI Feed, Try More, and Ask Fred docked on the right (`DockedAsk`, shared with the library).

**Channels are tags.** The library's left panel is the reference's: My Meetings, All Meetings, Voice Agent Meetings (disabled), Uploads, then "All channels". Channels are the existing tags, now creatable ahead of time (`POST /api/tags`, 409 on a duplicate name ignoring case) and deletable (`DELETE /api/tags/{id}` removes only the label). Uploads is a real filter (`GET /api/meetings?source=upload`). "Shared with me" shows an honest empty state because there is no sharing.

**The meeting page has its own chrome.** On `/meetings/<id>` the permanent sidebar and shell top bar are replaced by the reference's bar (menu, breadcrumb, actions, Share, bell, account); the menu opens the navigation as a drawer (`ShellContext`). Left rail: Smart Search, Insights, Transcript and Soundbites (not available). One `TranscriptPanel` instance serves all tabs through a `mode` prop so search, filters and scroll state are shared. Centre column: Notes / AI Skills.

**AI Skills are saved prompts.** `lib/skills.ts` is the single list. The AI Skills page is the reference's list-and-detail layout; Enable stores your choice in this browser and the skill appears on every meeting's AI Skills tab, where Run sends the prompt to that meeting's Ask Fred panel (a `window` event, since the two live in different parts of the tree). Typing `/` in any Ask Fred box lists them too.

**Profile panel opens on hover** (Base UI `openOnHover`, with a short close delay so the pointer can travel into it) and still works on click and keyboard.

**Analytics** was built from scratch because the reference page sits behind a paywall. It follows the shape visible in the blurred screenshot (two charts, an insight banner, four stat cards, then detail cards), using only data this app has. The Team tab is shown disabled.

## Free LLM providers

`LLM_BASE_URL` switches the client from the Anthropic SDK to any OpenAI-compatible `/chat/completions` endpoint, using `httpx` (already a dependency). Verified live against Groq with `openai/gpt-oss-120b` (the first model I tried, `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`, had been retired: the models endpoint is the way to check). Two real problems showed up only against a live model: it writes citations with a narrow no-break space (U+202F) and non-breaking hyphens in ranges, so `[#7 02:39]` and `[00:33-01:00]` did not parse and sources came back empty. Model output is now normalised in one place (`llm_client._tidy`) and both citation parsers accept ranges. Tests ignore a developer's `backend/.env`.

## Measured parity pass (sizes, spacing, layout)

The first two passes matched the look by eye and the result still read as a different product. This pass measured instead. The reference screenshots in `docs/reference/` are 2x captures of a 1470 px-wide window, so CSS pixels are native pixels / 2. I sampled colours and found element edges numerically (Pillow), then rendered each page here with headless Chrome at the same viewport and scale and compared the two side by side.

What the measurements changed:
- **Type is 14 px almost everywhere**, not 15. Widths of known strings ("Voice Agents", "Create Team", "Hosted by me"...) imply Inter at 13.4-14 px. Titles are 24 px (page) and 20 px (greetings).
- **Sidebar:** 232 px + 1 px border, rail 56 px; rows are 32 px high with a 1.5 px gap, groups pad 8 px and are split by 1 px `#292929` rules; 16 px icons with a 1.5 px stroke; active row `#292929`; avatar 20 px. The top bar is 52 px, the search box 319x34 at a fixed offset, Capture 125x32. The banner is 40 px.
- **Pages with a secondary column** (Meetings, AskFred) keep the sidebar as a 56 px rail and give the room to a full-height column (248 px channels / 279 px chats) that runs alongside the top bar. Settings and a single meeting have no sidebar or top bar of their own.
- **Collapsed rail:** hovering the avatar swaps it for the panel icon ("Expand sidebar"); hovering an expanded sidebar reveals the collapse icon.
- **Ask Fred panel** is 420 px (405 on a meeting) with emoji starter prompts, and different prompts on Home, the library and a meeting.
- **Colour tokens** corrected to the sampled values: text `#fafafb`, secondary `#aeaeb2`, tile `#b22d5b`, borders `#292929`/`#323235`.

Deliberate differences from the reference: Fireflies' logos (Gmail, Slack, store badges) are replaced with original marks; copy that would be untrue here ("free trial", "3 free meetings", "Consumes AI credits") says what this app does; features that do not exist are labelled, not faked. Pages without a reference screenshot (Tasks, Search, Integrations, Analytics) were restyled with the same tokens but not measured.

## Team settings, theme tokens, audio uploads

**Team settings are workspace defaults, labelled as such.** The Team toggle opens the reference's Team screens (Recording & Privacy, Compliance, AI Settings, Live Meeting, Rules, Teammates and groups) behind the "You're editing Teams settings" notice. Teams do not exist here, so each "Allow teammates to choose / Enable for all / Disable for all" choice is saved in a `team` settings section (validated, tested) but enforced on no one, and every page says so. The teammates list shows you as the only admin; Invite explains why it cannot work yet; Rules is the reference's empty state with an honest button.

**Colours are tokens now.** The measured pass wrote dark hex values straight into class names, so Light mode left half the UI dark. About 400 of them became theme tokens (`fg2`, `fg3`, `iris`, `chip`, `seg`...) with light values; dark mode is byte-for-byte the same colours.

**A recording can be uploaded on its own.** The big drop zone takes audio or video; the server sends it to the provider's `/audio/transcriptions` (Whisper) and feeds the result through the normal VTT path, so summaries, action items and Ask Fred all work. Whisper cannot tell speakers apart, so lines are labelled "Speaker". Whisper also invents short filler ("Thank you.") over trailing silence and stretches it across it; segments longer than 10 s with under half a word per second are dropped.

## Meeting page from a real Fireflies result (and where this app is better)

Uploading the sample recording to Fireflies showed the target layout: filter cards with counts, sentiment rows, a talk-time table with WPM, topic trackers, a summary-style picker, an outline with a timestamp on every point, action items by person, a rating card and "Continue from this meeting". All of that is built, with real data behind it: notes bullets link to the transcript line they came from (the line sharing the most words with the note, inside its chapter), tracker counts come from the transcript, and summary styles / "Refine" change the prompt (`summary_templates.py`).

**Flaws in the reference I fixed instead of copying.** It merged the three speakers of the sample into two and gave action items a meaningless "00:00". Here:
- **Identify speakers** reads the conversation with the AI model and re-labels the transcript. It first splits speech chunks into sentences (Whisper chunks often hold two people), asks for the *fewest* believable speakers, and merges neighbouring sentences by the same person back into turns. Action item links are remapped to the turn covering their moment. It cannot invent names nobody says, so the host stayed "Speaker 1" on the sample; rename in Edit.
- Action items show the timestamp of the moment they were said, or none, never a placeholder.
- Suggested questions are written from this meeting's summary (cached per summary version), with an outline-based fallback when no model is configured.

## Notes depth pass (nested points, figures, exact timestamps)

- **Why:** Fireflies' notes carry the specifics (0.4% crash rate, 1 in 20 logins, October 23rd) in nested bullets, each with a timestamp. Ours had one sentence per chapter.
- **Storage without a migration.** `Chapter.summary` now holds an indented bullet list: `- point {@ms}` with `  - detail` lines beneath. `{@ms}` is the transcript moment the point came from. `app/services/notes_format.py` is the single reader/writer; the frontend mirrors it in `lib/notes.ts` (`parseNotes`). Old plain-prose summaries still parse (each sentence becomes a point), so existing meetings keep working and the API schema is unchanged.
- **Model prompt** asks for 2-5 points per chapter with 1-3 details, terse note-taker phrasing, and forbids vague replacements or invented figures. Each point returns the `seq` of its source line, which becomes an exact timestamp; bad `seq` values drop only the moment, and a plain `summary` string from a model that ignores the schema is still accepted.
- **No-model fallback** picks the sentences with digits/dates/weekdays first and links each to the line it was said on.
- Search, Ask Fred and exports use `plain()` so the markers never show up in text.
- Points without a stored moment fall back to the old word-overlap lookup (`momentFor`), so every bullet still links to a real line.
